stories.evidence_status: Resume-supported claims, not independently verified; personal narrative details still need confirmation.

strengths: Strong customer-facing anchor with a clear before/after.

Threshold calibration, exception checks, real tradeoff, and measurement window.

assessment.stakes: Financial-record accuracy is plausible context; audit obligations, cutoff dates, and impact must be confirmed.
assessment.ownership: The resume says designed and launched; it does not establish sole engineering ownership.
assessment.decision: LangGraph and confidence routing are named, but the rejected alternative and rationale are absent.
assessment.tradeoff: Automation versus review workload is a useful discussion; actual threshold error rates are missing.
assessment.measurement: Define reconciliation effort, turnaround start/end, sample size, and whether all metrics share the same cohort.

What did it cost per record?
How would you build it on AWS only?
delivery: Open with turnaround, then briefly explain GL/AP/AR as financial records.
Paint one actual reviewer decision; do not invent a customer quote, audit event, or zero-error claim.

For engineers, explain confidence routing, independent validation, and safe replay. For executives, explain the reported turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours and the reviewer decision boundary. Confirm the measurement and stakeholder acceptance; do not claim audit compliance or zero errors.
stories.draft: At MSRcosmos, I worked on moving 10,000+ financial records from Sage X3 to Sage Intacct across 12 client entities. The records covered the general ledger, accounts payable, and accounts receivable. Reconciliation created a substantial manual workload. My task was to automate that workflow while keeping a clear path for human review when a record needed attention. I built the multi-agent workflow with the Claude API and LangGraph, and connected it to Sage REST APIs through MCP tool calling. I designed confidence-based routing: records above the threshold could auto-approve, while lower-confidence records went to a reviewer. This focused human effort on exceptions rather than treating every record the same way. I containerized the system with Docker for cloud-agnostic deployment across AWS, Azure, and GCP. Manual reconciliation fell 68%, and 83% of records auto-approved. Turnaround decreased from 3 days to 5.5 hours. The central design lesson is that useful automation needs an explicit boundary between what the system can process and what a person should review.

stories.draft: At Oracle, I worked on NSX observability for a platform serving 37,000+ enterprise tenants. During an incident, detecting an API failure is only the starting point; the engineer still needs to understand the likely cause and the next action. My work was to improve that diagnosis path through real-time API diagnostics across 1M+ endpoints. I instrumented the high-throughput event streams so API failure evidence was available in real time. I added automatic root-cause tags for 400- and 500-series failures, connecting the failure signal with useful diagnostic context. I included runbook context so the on-call engineer could move from seeing an error to investigating and mitigating it. The important change was making the information actionable, rather than simply producing more telemetry. P1 MTTR dropped from 94 to 26 minutes, a 72% reduction. The lesson is that operational tooling should shorten the path from signal to action. A dashboard has value when it helps someone recover the service.

stories.title: SLO alerting, 41% fewer false pages
stories.evidence_status: Resume-supported claims, not independently verified; personal narrative details still need confirmation.

assessment.ownership: Architected the stack is resume language; dashboard, alert, and rollout responsibilities need boundaries.
assessment.decision: A CPU or memory threshold is not by itself a user-facing SLO; explain the actual indicator.
assessment.tradeoff: Lower noise can hide failures; describe the chosen sensitivity and verification.
assessment.measurement: 41% reduction needs before/after page counts, labels, measurement windows, and comparable traffic.

probes: How did you pick the targets?
How did you handle cardinality across 37,000+ tenants?
Did you use burn-rate alerting?
delivery: Use one noisy alert and the signal that replaced it.

For engineers, explain the actual SLI, target, alert sensitivity, and missed-incident checks. For executives, connect 41% fewer false-positive pages to attention available for real incidents, without claiming measured productivity or customer benefit that was not recorded.
stories.draft: The NSX environment served 37,000+ enterprise tenants. Static thresholds can produce pages when a resource crosses a limit without clearly explaining whether the service is meeting its objectives. That makes alert quality as important as alert coverage. I architected the Prometheus and Grafana observability stack and moved alerting toward service-level objectives, using CPU, memory, and p99 latency signals. I organized the monitoring around the service objectives and the signals engineers needed to investigate degradation. I built 47 dashboards and alert rules across the observability stack. Dashboards provided the investigation view, while alert rules determined when an engineer needed to take action. I treated the resource signals and latency together: CPU or memory alone does not describe the entire experience of a service. False-positive on-call pages decreased 41%. The design lesson is to make alerts actionable and tied to service behavior. Reducing noise only helps if the system still brings meaningful problems to the on-call engineer.

stories.draft: At Oracle, configuration errors could be discovered during deployment or after a change reached production. Finding the same issue earlier in the delivery process gives engineers a chance to correct it before it becomes an operational problem. My task was to build scripted pre-deployment validation into the Jenkins CI/CD workflow. I shipped a CLI toolchain that ran the validation checks as part of CI, so configuration problems could fail before the deployment stage. I made the checks part of the delivery workflow rather than leaving validation as an informal step an engineer had to remember. The toolchain was adopted by 4 engineering teams across NSX. That gave multiple teams a common way to catch configuration errors earlier while continuing to use Jenkins for delivery. Release cycles became 34% shorter, and the failed-deployment rate fell from 11% to 4%. The lesson is that reliability can improve developer speed. A useful validation mechanism prevents downstream rework and makes the safer path part of the normal workflow.

stories.title: NetSuite search latency down 30%

For engineers, explain one query plan, index choice, write cost, and rollout. For executives, explain median search page load falling from 840 ms to 588 ms and ask which user workflow matters. Do not invent hardware savings or increased revenue.
stories.draft: At Oracle, I worked on search performance at enterprise data volumes. A slow page can have several causes, so the important starting point was to understand how the database was executing the queries behind the search. My task was to improve the database access path driving that page-load latency. I profiled the query plans to identify the SQL responsible for full scans. I restructured indexes on the hot predicates and rewrote the SQL driving those scans. The goal was to make the access path better match the filters the search actually used. I focused on the query plan and index design because reducing unnecessary reads addresses the work the database is doing, rather than assuming that a larger instance is the answer. P50 page-load latency improved from 840 to 588 milliseconds, a 30% reduction in median page load through a better database access path. The lesson is to diagnose the access pattern before selecting a scaling solution. The right architecture recommendation starts with evidence about the bottleneck.

stories.draft: At Oracle, release surges created changing demand for NSX services. Keeping the services responsive required both containerized deployment and a scaling policy that reflected the workload, rather than looking only at CPU utilization. My work combined Docker and Kubernetes containerization with horizontal autoscaling driven by custom Prometheus metrics. I containerized the NSX services on OCI using Docker and Kubernetes. I used custom Prometheus metrics as inputs to horizontal autoscaling instead of relying on CPU alone. Resource utilization is useful, but it is not a complete explanation of whether a service is keeping up with its demand. I connected the scaling behavior to the service latency objective, keeping the discussion focused on the performance the system needed to preserve through a surge. The services held their p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges. The lesson is to scale from a signal that represents the workload and to evaluate the result against a service objective. My implementation experience here was on OCI.

stories.title: DQN training stall, 40% shorter runs

stories.draft: In sports analytics research at USC, I prototyped a reinforcement-learning agent for NFL fourth-down decisions using 420K plays. The agent used expected points added in its reward design, and each training run took 52 minutes. My work included improving the training pipeline so each experiment spent less time on data handling. I vectorized replay-buffer sampling, moving that work away from inefficient per-item processing. I removed a data-loader stall. Both changes targeted the path feeding training rather than changing the problem into a request for more compute. I kept the performance result separate from the model-quality result: making the pipeline quicker and improving decision agreement are different accomplishments with different measurements. Training time fell to 31 minutes per run, about a 40% reduction in runtime. Separately, agreement with EPA-optimal calls improved from 68% to 74% on held-out 2024 drives. The lesson is to understand the work surrounding model computation. Data movement and sampling can limit experiment speed even when the model itself gets most of the attention.

stories.draft: At USC AI Trust Lab, I am using Llama 3.3 70B to label caseworker notes. Annotation needs a consistent definition of each label, and the model needs a path to escalate the cases it cannot handle confidently. My task is to turn that into a pipeline with a rubric, confidence scores, and human-in-the-loop review. I am building the rubric-based labeling workflow on Llama 3.3 70B, giving the annotation process explicit criteria rather than asking the model for an unconstrained answer. I am adding confidence scoring that routes low-confidence cases to domain experts. The model handles labeling, while the review path brings in human judgment where it matters. I am keeping the design centered on three responsibilities: produce a label, expose uncertainty, and route the cases that need attention. The work is ongoing. The pipeline labels notes, scores confidence, and routes lower-confidence cases to experts, giving the annotation workflow a concrete path from an initial model label to domain-expert review. The design lesson is that confidence should guide review, not stand in for proof that a model is correct. The escalation path belongs in the architecture.

stories.title: ModelScope quantization study
stories.evidence_status: Resume-supported claims, not independently verified; personal narrative details still need confirmation.

assessment.tradeoff: Quality, memory, throughput, latency, and hardware compatibility can change the choice.
assessment.measurement: Clarify model, batch size, sequence length, warmup, repeats, memory definition, and INT8 comparator.

delivery: Say in this T4 benchmark before stating the result.

For engineers, explain the exact model, workload, measurement method, comparator, and quality constraint. For executives, describe the tested resource-versus-quality choice and the need for customer-specific evaluation. No production cost saving or universal precision recommendation is established.
stories.draft: I benchmarked Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B on a T4 GPU to understand quantization tradeoffs. A smaller memory footprint is only useful if the model also meets the quality and performance requirements of its workload. My task was to compare configurations across latency, throughput, peak memory, and evaluation quality instead of selecting precision from a single metric. I tested 8 configurations spanning FP16, INT8, INT4, and NF4, using PyTorch and CUDA to profile inference. I measured the resource and performance dimensions, then used a Pareto sweep to compare tradeoffs. That makes it possible to identify configurations that improve one requirement without ignoring the others. I included MMLU as a quality check alongside the performance measurements, keeping the conclusion tied to the benchmark setup. INT4 used 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, while sustaining 13.7 tokens per second and keeping MMLU within a point of baseline. The lesson is to benchmark the workload before recommending a model configuration, then choose a configuration that meets its quality, performance, and operational requirements.

For engineers, explain merge keys, deletes, late arrivals, correctness, and the meaning of full refresh. For executives, explain the 22-minute reported refresh in relation to the customer freshness requirement once confirmed. Native AWS equivalents remain proposed designs.
stories.draft: At MSRcosmos, the ERP agents depended on financial data from Databricks workspaces across AWS, Azure, and GCP. The data pipeline was part of making the agent workflow useful: the agents needed the underlying records available for processing. My task was to automate the nightly feed and stage the financial tables into Delta Lake. I built the feed with PySpark, bringing the 17 tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake. I used partition pruning to reduce unnecessary reads, and incremental merges to incorporate changes without treating every update as a complete rewrite. I automated the feed across the cloud workspaces, connecting the data-engineering layer with the multi-agent ERP system. The processing choices addressed how much data the job needed to read and update. The full refresh held at 22 minutes. The lesson is that an AI application still depends on its data foundation. Efficient ingestion and clear refresh behavior matter just as much as the agent logic that uses the data.

gaps.title: A real failure or mistake
gaps.why: No existing story establishes something you owned that went wrong, its consequence, and your change in behavior. A success with a difficult starting point is not automatically a failure story.
prompts: What did I decide or miss, and what evidence shows it was wrong?
Who was affected, what did I disclose, and what did I do first?
What changed afterward, and how do I know the prevention mechanism worked?

gaps.title: A real disagreement and commitment
gaps.why: No documented disagreement exists. The CLI adoption and SLO redesign are only places to search your memory, not proof that resistance occurred.
prompts: Who disagreed and what was their strongest reason?
What data or customer need did I bring, and who made the decision?
If my proposal lost, what did I do to commit to the chosen direction?

gaps.title: A real person who grew through your help
gaps.why: Four-team adoption does not demonstrate coaching. Show a person's starting point, your deliberate intervention, and what they could do independently afterward.
prompts: Who did I help and what could they not do initially?
What specific feedback, pairing, exercise, or review did I provide?
What did they do independently later, and what evidence shows progress?

delivery_drills.title: Make one real scene visible
steps: Name the affected user or stakeholder and the exact workflow.
State what could go wrong or what was delayed; use a real example, not an invented crisis.
Explain the choice you owned, the alternative, and the constraint in plain words.

delivery_drills.title: Rehearse a 90-second core
steps: Spend roughly 20 seconds on context and task, 50 on actions and reasoning, and 20 on result and lesson; adjust naturally.
Say one main metric with baseline and unit. Define acronyms briefly.
Record yourself, replay once, and remove any line that does not clarify the decision. These timings are a practice drill.

delivery_drills.title: Prepare a deeper follow-up
steps: Spend up to three practice minutes explaining the rejected alternative, a failure mode, and the measurement method.
Answer what you actually did before describing a hypothetical AWS equivalent.
If a value was not measured, say so and explain how you would measure it now.

delivery_drills.title: Build breadth across episodes
steps: Practise S1/S2/S4/S5 as anchors and S3/S6/S8/S11/S12 as technical alternatives.
Count S7 as another S1 angle. S12 shares the ERP program even when its technical decision is distinct.
Fill the failure, disagreement, and mentoring gaps from real memory; keep S9/S10 as ongoing design discussions until outcomes or accepted milestones exist.

delivery_drills.title: One story for engineers and executives
steps: Technical audience: give S1 a 90-second explanation of the financial migration, your ownership, routing decision, rejected alternative, validation, failure recovery, and reported result. Confirm each mechanism rather than borrowing a proposed AWS design as history.

Executive audience: give S1 a 30-second version. Proposed wording: I worked on financial migration across 12 entities. The workflow combined automation with human review, and reported turnaround fell from 3 days to 5.5 hours. Before using it, be ready to state the measurement period and your own contribution..

As an alternative, use S2: engineers need actual diagnostic signals and false-tag handling; executives need the reported P1 recovery change from 94 to 26 minutes and the affected workflow. Confirm the measurement and customer impact before using either version.

Rehearse a handoff to a sales partner: ask what business objective, decision-maker, constraint, and success measure the customer has. This is a proposed role-play, not a claim of prior sales collaboration.
